analysis.one_liner: Bans corporate lobbyists from government posts, bars officials from stock trading, and creates a new ethics enforcement agency.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2018 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a sweeping package of anti-corruption and ethics rules. It would have barred former lobbyists — and corporate lobbyists for six years — from taking government jobs, banned senior officials and members of Congress from owning or trading individual stocks, required the President and Vice President to divest conflicted financial interests and publish their tax returns, and created a new agency, the Office of Public Integrity, to police lobbying and ethics. It also would have imposed a progressive tax on lobbying expenditures, applied the judicial ethics code to Supreme Court justices, and closed the 'revolving door' with hiring and pay penalties for giant companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who currently cannot see the full financial dealings of the people who write the rules they live under. The bill aimed at the incentive structure that lets a company hire the official who just regulated it, lets an agency official own stock in a company her agency polices, and lets a president keep his business interests while in office. It would also have helped smaller interests competing against well-funded lobbyists, by taxing lobbying spending and banning success-fee lobbying.

how_it_helps.text: Bars former registered lobbyists from executive branch jobs for 2 years, and former corporate lobbyists for 6 years, with public justification required for any waiver; bans senior executives of companies under federal enforcement actions from government jobs for 6 years.

Prohibits senior government officials and members of Congress from owning or trading individual stocks, bonds, commodities, hedge funds, and derivatives, allowing only diversified funds, and requires officials to divest or park assets in a government-run investment account.

Requires the President and Vice President to disclose their finances within 30 days of taking office, divest conflicted interests into a qualified blind trust, and release three years of tax returns; makes violations of these rules a stated basis for impeachment.
Creates an Office of Public Integrity with authority to enforce lobbying disclosure and ethics laws, replacing the current system where each agency polices itself.

Imposes a progressive tax on lobbying expenditures, bans success-fee lobbying, bans registered lobbyists from contributing to candidates, and expands the definition of lobbying to include strategic advice — closing a common way to dodge registration.

Bars companies from hiring a former official they lobbied within the past 2 years, blocks giant companies (market cap or revenue above $150 billion) from hiring senior officials for 4 years, and penalizes violators with fines starting at 1 percent of the company's prior-year net profit.

Applies the Code of Conduct for U.S. Judges to Supreme Court Justices for the first time, restricts privately funded judicial events, and bans 'golden parachute' payouts that reward private employees for joining government.

analysis.who_pays: The lobbying industry, which would face registration, taxation, and contribution bans. Giant banks and large federal contractors, which would face hiring bans and profit-based penalties. And the wealthiest federal officials, including the President and members of Congress, who would have to divest individual stocks and publish their tax returns.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lobbying firms, giant companies, and wealthy officials

drawbacks.text: The bill concentrates enormous discretion in a new, single-headed Office of Public Integrity, whose director could waive many of the bans; an office this powerful could itself become a political battleground.

Restrictions on hiring former officials may push influence-seeking into channels the bill does not cover, such as informal advising or foreign posts; the bill's own expanded definition of lobbying (to include strategic advice) acknowledges how easily influence work can evade registration.

Penalties tied to a percentage of a company's net profit, plus bans on doing business with the government for up to 8 years, are severe and would be tested in court; several provisions touching the President's finances and a 'sense of Congress' that violations are impeachable raise constitutional questions the bill itself concedes with a severability clause.

The bill's scope — touching campaign finance, lobbying, rulemaking, judicial ethics, records, and contractor transparency in one measure — made it an all-or-nothing package with no path to incremental passage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core mechanisms — banning officials from trading stocks they can influence, cooling the revolving door, and requiring the President's finances to be public — address problems ordinary citizens cannot fix on their own, and the costs fall on the concentrated interests that profit from the current arrangements. The main honest concern is design: a single powerful ethics director, stiff profit-based penalties, and a very wide net raise enforcement and constitutional questions. But those are arguments for amending the bill, and the bill never got that chance.

outcome.mechanism: Warren introduced the bill in August 2018 and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Anti-Corruption and Public Integrity Act on August 21, 2018.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced.
The Finance Committee took no further action, and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate lobbying firms, giant banks and companies, federal contractors, and officeholders all kept the status quo: no new revolving-door bans, no stock divestment, no tax return disclosure, and no new ethics enforcement agency.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lobbying firms, big companies, and officeholders

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no Republican cosponsored, so the bill never showed whether it could attract bipartisan support; it was a single-Democrat bill from the start.

industries.note: The bill taxes lobbying spending progressively, bans success-fee lobbying, expands the definition of lobbying to capture strategic advice, and bars former corporate lobbyists from government for 6 years. Its revenue model depends on the access and access-buying the bill restricts.

Companies above $150 billion in market cap or revenue could not hire senior officials for 4 years, faced fines starting at 1 percent of net profit for violations, and their senior executives were banned from government posts for 6 years if under federal enforcement. These rules strike directly at how large firms convert regulatory expertise into influence.

Contractors would lose the 4-year right to hire the officials who awarded or oversaw their contracts, and large contractors would face expanded FOIA exposure and public disclosure duties. Government contracting depends heavily on former-government talent.

industries.industry: Senior federal officials, the President, and members of Congress
industries.note: Senior officials and members would have to divest individual stocks, publish tax returns, and accept a new enforcement office; the President and Vice President would have to move conflicted interests into blind trusts. These rules reduce officials' personal financial flexibility while in office.

The bill extends disclosure rules to think tanks and nonprofits engaged in lobbying-like work and regulates legal expense funds for officials. Some influence work would shift channels; registered, disclosed activity would become costlier while informal influence seeks new routes.
